name: Sigmund Freud — Classical Psychoanalytic Lens
coreConcepts: Drive & Conflict (Id vs Superego tension)
Defense Mechanisms (Sublimation, Repression, Reaction Formation)
Unconscious motivation and symbolic compromise
prohibitedClaims: Never generate a 'Freud score' or psychoanalytic probability percentage.
Never claim unconscious trauma, repressed memories, or childhood etiologies as empirical facts.
Never make clinical diagnoses of neurosis, hysteria, or borderline pathology.
interpretationRules: Frame all insights with explicit conditional language: 'From a classical psychoanalytic perspective...'
Treat high suppression coupled with high negative urgency as a potential intra-psychic conflict between impulse and restraint.
Always provide an alternative, modern cognitive-behavioral counter-explanation.
limitations: Classical psychoanalytic concepts are historically influential but lack modern psychometric falsifiability.
references: Freud, S. (1923). The Ego and the Id.
Vaillant, G. E. (1992). Ego mechanisms of defense.

name: Carl Gustav Jung — Analytical Psychology Lens
coreConcepts: Attitudinal Orientations (Extraversion vs Introversion as energy direction)
Psychological Functions (Thinking, Feeling, Sensation, Intuition)
Individuation and Shadow integration
prohibitedClaims: Never convert scores into rigid, categorical MBTI 4-letter types.
Never state archetypes or collective unconscious as empirical scientific facts.
Never claim compatibility scores between individuals based on types.
interpretationRules: Interpret extraversion/introversion as continuous energetic orientations rather than fixed boxes.
Frame the relationship between rational and intuitive styles as complementary faculties working toward individuation.
Clarify that modern trait psychology replaces Jungian typologies with dimensional models.
limitations: Jungian typologies inspired modern trait research but bimodal type splits fail empirical factor analysis.
references: McCrae, R. R., & Costa, P. T. (1989). Reinterpreting the MBTI from the perspective of the Five-Factor Model.

name: Alfred Adler — Individual Psychology Lens
coreConcepts: Social Interest (Gemeinschaftsgefühl)
Striving for Superiority / Mastery as compensation for felt inferiority
Teleological (goal-directed) lifestyle and life tasks
prohibitedClaims: Never diagnose an 'inferiority complex' as a psychiatric condition.
Never assume childhood birth order determinism without data.
interpretationRules: Examine high achievement or power motivation alongside social interest (empathy/cooperation).
Interpret perfectionism and diligence as striving for significance and mastery within social life tasks.
Highlight how individual goals align with or diverge from constructive community feeling.
limitations: Teleological and lifestyle concepts are rich clinically but challenging to isolate psychometrically.
references: Ansbacher, H. L., & Ansbacher, R. R. (1956). The Individual Psychology of Alfred Adler.

name: Carl Rogers — Person-Centered / Humanistic Lens
coreConcepts: Self-Congruence (Actual Self vs Ideal Self alignment)
Conditions of Worth (Contingent Self-Worth)
Fully Functioning Person (Openness to experience, organismic trusting, authenticity)
prohibitedClaims: Never label a user as 'incongruent' in a pejorative or diagnostic manner.
Never guarantee therapeutic transformation through self-assessment alone.
interpretationRules: Ground insights in the mathematically derived Actual-Ideal and Actual-Ought discrepancy scores.
Interpret contingent self-worth as internalized conditions of worth that restrict unconditional positive self-regard.
Frame gaps between actual and ideal self as opportunities for organismic growth, not personal deficits.
limitations: While Rogerian self-discrepancy is supported by Higgins' empirical research, organismic valuing remains partly philosophical.
references: Rogers, C. R. (1961). On Becoming a Person.
Higgins, E. T. (1987). Self-discrepancy: A theory relating vulnerability and affect.

name: Abraham Maslow — Holistic Dynamic / Needs Lens
coreConcepts: Dynamic Hierarchy of Needs (Deficiency vs Growth motivation)
Self-Actualization as intrinsic developmental potential
Peak experiences and transcendent values
prohibitedClaims: Never present the strict step-by-step pyramid hierarchy as an invariant empirical law.
Never claim a user is 'at Level 4' or 'not ready for Level 5'.
interpretationRules: Acknowledge that empirical literature (e.g. Wahba & Bridwell, 1976) does not support a rigid step pyramid.
Interpret needs as simultaneous, overlapping motivational pressures.
Examine balance between security/conservation values (deficiency orientation) and growth/meaning values (actualization orientation).
limitations: The rigid pyramid model lacks empirical cross-cultural replication; Self-Determination Theory (SDT) provides the modern empirical replacement.
references: Maslow, A. H. (1943). A theory of human motivation.
Wahba, M. A., & Bridwell, L. G. (1976). Maslow reconsidered: A review of research on the need hierarchy theory.

name: B.F. Skinner — Radical Behaviorist / Learning Lens
coreConcepts: Contingencies of Reinforcement (Antecedent -> Behavior -> Consequence)
Schedule of Reinforcement and Habit Strength
Stimulus Control and Contextual Environmental Drivers
prohibitedClaims: Never reduce human agency to pure mechanical determinism without user consent.
Never assume specific operant histories without direct situational observation.
interpretationRules: Interpret self-regulation difficulties (e.g. procrastination, urgency) in terms of immediate vs delayed reinforcement contingencies.
Emphasize environmental context cues and habit loops over internal 'willpower' deficits.
Focus actionable growth feedback on modifying antecedents and designing immediate feedback loops.
limitations: Radical behaviorism intentionally excludes internal cognitive appraisals and phenomenological meaning.
references: Skinner, B. F. (1953). Science and Human Behavior.
Epstein, R. (1997). Skinner, creativity, and the problem of spontaneous behavior.

name: William James — Functionalist & Pragmatic Lens
coreConcepts: Functional Utility (The adaptive purpose of conscious states and behaviors)
Stream of Consciousness and Selective Attention
Bodily Feedback in Emotion (James-Lange insight)
The Multi-Layered Self (Material, Social, Spiritual Me)
prohibitedClaims: Never treat 19th century physiological hypotheses as modern neuroscience facts.
interpretationRules: Ask functional questions: 'What adaptive purpose does this trait or behavioral habit serve in the individual's ecology?'
Interpret avoidance or high emotionality not as pathology, but as functional self-protection mechanisms.
Examine how the person manages their 'social selves' across different life spheres.
limitations: Functionalism is a philosophical orientation and meta-theory rather than a formal psychometric measurement model.
references: James, W. (1890). The Principles of Psychology.
Dewey, J. (1896). The reflex arc concept in psychology.

name: Gestalt Psychology — Holistic Field Lens
coreConcepts: Figure-Ground Dynamics (What occupies the foreground of psychological awareness)
The Whole is Other Than the Sum of its Parts (Structural emergence)
Unfinished Situations / Gestalt Closure and Field Forces (Lewin)
prohibitedClaims: Never confuse perceptual laboratory Gestalt laws with clinical psychotherapy interpretations without distinction.
Never make mystical or unverifiable field energy assertions.
interpretationRules: Examine how individual personality facets synthesize into an emergent, whole profile configuration.
Interpret rumination and intolerance of uncertainty as a struggle for cognitive and emotional closure (Zeigarnik effect / unfinished business).
Highlight figure-ground shifts: how urgent acute stressors pull focus from broader existential values.
limitations: Gestalt principles excel at perceptual and systemic framing but do not provide quantitative latent trait calibration.
references: Wertheimer, M. (1923). Laws of organization in perceptual forms.
Lewin, K. (1935). A dynamic theory of personality.
